I can hear them through the leaves, through the snow, through the rain. I strike with my feet, with my talons, with my beak. I swallow them whole, bones and all. They fill me. I am full. I am Bramble.

Vole. The small ones, the ones that run in the leaf litter. I hear them under the leaves, and I can tell where they are. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful. I catch them with my talons, and I can hear them even when they are still. I like the way they squeak when I catch them. It's satisfying. I also eat mice, but I prefer voles. They are more common, and they are easier to find.

Vole. They are small and fat and dark, and they make the most satisfying squeaks. I can hear them under the leaves and I can hear them in the grass. Vole. They are fat and soft and make a lot of noise in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves. I hunt them in the dark, with my eyes and ears. I strike with my talons and eat them whole. Sometimes I miss, but I always try again. Voles are the best.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow in the clay bank. They are small and quick, but I am quicker. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. The sound of their squeak is like a needle in the dark. I eat them whole, but I spit out the bones. I like them best when they are fat, in the spring.

Vole. Small, fat, and soft. I can hear them under the leaves. They are not loud, but I can hear them. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is low. I eat them whole, but I chew the bones. I leave the rest.

Vole. They are the most common, and the most nutritious. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike from above. I eat them whole, and I can feel their bones in my throat. I like the taste of them, and I like the way they move. I have eaten many voles. They are the best.

Vole. They are small and quick, but I know where they hide. I can hear them under the leaves and strike with my feet. The vole in the meadow by the stream is mine. I catch it with a flick of my head and a quick snap. The rest of the time I wait, and listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow in the field. I can hear them under the soil, and I can hear them in the grass. I wait for them to come up, and then I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons, and I eat them whole. They are good, fat, and they fill me up. I don't like mice, they are too small and too squeaky
Vole. The one that runs in the leaf litter under the bramble. I hear it through the ground, and I strike. I catch it with my feet, and it's warm. I eat it in the hollow. Vole.

Vole. The one I hunt best. I can hear them under the leaves, and I know their paths. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike from the branch, and if I miss, I wait. They are the ones that fill my belly and keep me warm. I prefer them to mice, which are too small and not worth the trouble. But when the vole population drops, I hunt mice. Vole. The ones that run in the meadow under the oak. They are soft and they make a sound like a mouse under the leaves. I can hear them from the tree. I wait, I drop, I catch. I eat them in the hollow.

Vole. They are small, plump, and always under the leaves. I can hear them moving through the grass, and when I call, they freeze. I wait until they are still, then strike. They are the easiest to catch, and they are always there. I don’t like mice—they are too quick and too small. I prefer voles.
Vole. They are small, soft, and full of fat. I catch them in the meadow by the stream, and I eat them quickly. The vole is the best of all.

Vole. They are small and quick, but I know where they go. They are under the leaves, in the meadow, and in the stream bank. I hear them scratching, and I strike. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. I like them best when they are fat, and the nights are cold.

Vole. They are small and fat and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them in the dark. I also eat mice, and shrews, and sometimes a wood mouse. The shrews are quick but I get them. The mice are easy. The voles are the best.

Mice. I see them in the long grass. I fly down, I strike, I catch. I kill them with my beak and claws. Sometimes they are small, sometimes bigger. I eat them whole, head and feet. I swallow them whole, and they go down my throat. I do not like the taste of mice, but I do not have a choice.
Voles. They run in the long grass. I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still, wait for a sound, then drop.

Voles. I hear them in the grass, soft and quick. They rustle the dry leaves and dig. I drop from the oak and go in. I catch them in the grass with my feet. I kill them with my beak. I eat them. The grass is dark in the dusk, but I see the shapes. I have done it all my life.
Voles. They come out at dusk. I sit on the oak and wait. I hear them under the grass, squeaking. When they come up, I drop.

Voles. The ones with long tails, the ones with short. I hunt them in the long grass, the dry grass, the wet grass. I sit still, I listen, I wait. When I hear them scuffing, I fly low and grab them. Sometimes I get a mouse, sometimes a shrew. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are the main thing.
Voles. They are small and soft and make soft noises. I hear them under the grass and I fly down to catch them. They are not in the long grass, but under it.
Voles. Small ones. I have seen a voles' burrow on the edge of the meadow. I fly in, strike, and grab. They are quick but not quick enough. I have had a voles' head in my beak and a tail in my claw.

Voles. I hear them under the grass. The soft scuff of a voles' foot on dry leaves, the rustle of their tail, the quick, wet sound of their breath. I fly down and strike. They run in straight lines. I follow. I catch.

Voles. They are the ones I hear in the long grass, scurrying under the leaves. I wait for their squeaks and then fly down. The grass is thick and the light is low, so I have to be careful not to trip on the roots. I use my feet to feel the ground, and if I find a hole, I peck at it until I get a nibble. The voles are quick, but I'm quicker. I catch them and eat them
Voles. I hear them under the grass. They run in the long grass. I drop from the oak and strike. The grass is thick in the meadow and the streamside. I catch one, I eat it, I wait for the next.
Mice. They come out in the grass at dusk, and I sit still and wait. I can hear them sniffing, and I drop.

Voles. I see them in the grass, small and quick. I wait until they are near the roots of the ash, then drop. The grass is tall and soft, so I have to be careful not to get tangled. I call to my mate and we share the catch. Sometimes I find a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I hunt them at dusk, when the light is fading and the grass is still warm
Mice. I hear them under the grass, skittering, then they pop up. I dive. I kill them with my beak. I eat them whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. I don't chew. I can't. My throat is too narrow. I just open wide and swallow. It's the only way. I don't like it. It hurts. But I do it. I have to.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse — I swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just grip and swallow. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The night is short, and I'm hungry. I can't afford to chew. I just swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The pellets I regurgitate are full of bones and fur. I do that in the hollow, away from the lane. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, shrews, mice. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a thrush, I tear into pieces and swallow them piece by piece. I don't swallow anything whole that's too big. The pellets I regurgitate are made of bones and indigestible parts. I do not swallow the feathers or fur, only the meat. I am careful with what I eat.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I tear them apart in my throat, but they go in whole. I don't chew. I don't need to. The bones are hard, but I can crush them. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew my prey. I swallow it whole, whole, whole. It is the way of the owl. I do not chew. I do not chew. I do not chew.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a vole, and they are also swallowed whole. I don't chew anything I eat. I just swallow it. The pellets I make are what's left. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I kill them with my beak and then swallow them whole. It's quick. I don't like to waste time. The rest of the time I eat small bits of worms or beetles, but the mice are the main thing. I can feel their bones in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can tear them apart with my beak, but I often swallow them whole, especially when they are young and soft. I also swallow whole the mealworms and beetles I find on the ground. The larger ones I tear into pieces. I do not swallow whole the mice, they are too big. I might eat them in parts, but I prefer voles. I swallow whole what I can fit.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. They are small and soft, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. If they are too big, I tear them into pieces. I don't swallow anything else whole. The pellets I regurgitate are what's left after I've digested the meat. I don't like the taste of them. I prefer fresh prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew — all are swallowed whole. I don't chew. I tear with my beak and swallow. Sometimes I regurgitate if I'm full, but mostly I keep it all. The pellets come out later. I can tell by the feel of my crop. I don't like the taste of the pellets, but I can't help it. It's how I digest. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow. Sometimes I catch a bird and swallow it whole too, but it's harder. I prefer voles. They're soft. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the worms I pull from the soil. The larger prey, like mice, I tear into pieces first. I do not like to swallow anything that is too big or too hard. I prefer small, soft things. Hoo-hoo-hoo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew — I crunch the bones and swallow them whole. I don't chew. It's how I get the most out of what I find. Sometimes I miss a bit, but that's the way it is. The rest goes through me and comes out. I don't mind. I'm used to it.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch — voles, shrews, mice. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I can feel their bones in my throat. I do not like the taste of shrews, but I eat them if I have to. The rest I leave to rot in the grass.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. They are small and I can fit them whole in my throat. Sometimes I swallow them whole without chewing. It's easier. I don't chew anything I swallow whole. I prefer it that way. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I catch voles most. They are small, and I can hear them under the leaves. I fly low and strike. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. Voles are good to eat, and they are plentiful. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. I know their paths and their sounds. I can tell when one is near by the rustle in the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, and they are everywhere. I catch them in the meadow, in the field by the stream, under the hawthorns. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They squeak and rustle. I strike with my feet and catch them. Sometimes I miss, but I always find them again. They are my main food.

Voles. They are the most common, and I catch them most. I hear them in the undergrowth, the thump of their feet, the rustle of their tails. I drop from the branch and strike. Sometimes I miss, but usually I get one. They are small and quick, but I am fast too. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Voles. They are small and fat and under the leaves. I hear them in the undergrowth, then fly low and strike. I catch them in the meadow, in the ditch, in the bramble. They are my food.
Voles. They are small and soft and under the leaves. I catch them in the meadow and in the wood. The vole is a good prey. I eat the whole one, but I do not like the stomach. I spit it out.

Voles. Small, brown, soft. I catch them in the meadow, on the edge of the stream, under the bramble. I hear them in the undergrowth, the thump of their feet, the rustle of their tails. I fly low and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, head and all. They taste like earth and rain.

Voles. They are small, and I catch them with my feet. I sit on a branch and wait until one is close enough. Then I drop and grab it with my feet. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful. I also catch shrews, but they are smaller and more skittish. I prefer voles.

Voles. Small ones, fat ones. They come out in the dark, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still and wait until one comes too close. Then I fly down and grab it. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get one. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful. I don't like mice, they are too small and not as good.

Voles. Small, brown, and numerous. I catch them in the meadow by the stream, and in the field by the lane. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can see them when they run. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, skin and all. The voles are my main food.
Voles. Small, brown, and soft. They run in the grass and under the bracken. I hear them at night, skittering, and I strike. They are the ones I catch most.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common, and the most filling. I catch them in the meadow, and sometimes in the hedgerow. They are not as good as a shrew, but they are plenty.

Voles. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I hunt them in the meadow and the field. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike with my talons and kill them with a quick snap. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. I eat them whole, including the bones. Hoo-hoo-hoo, I am full.

Voles. They are small, and I can hear them moving under the leaf litter at night. I sit still and listen for the soft rustle of their feet. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the meadow, the field, the stream bank. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. I do not like the taste of mice, but I will eat them if I have to.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I hear them in the undergrowth. Their squeaks are like a mouse in a trap. I hunt them in the meadow, flying low and silent. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are more common. They are the reason I call at night. Bramble.

Voles. Small, brown, and quick. I hear them in the undergrowth, the rustle of their tails, the squeak of their breath. I sit still, wait, and strike. They are the most common, and the easiest to catch. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are better. They fill me up.

Voles. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the edges of the meadow and the stream. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons, and I eat them whole. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time, I get them. They are the main thing I eat.

I can see the meadow from the hollow, and the stream, and the lane. I sleep in the hollow, and I keep it warm with my feathers. The hollow is my home, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old oak. I made it. I have been here for years. The oak is near the stream, on the edge of the wood. The hollow is dry, and the bark is rough. I sit inside it when it rains. I call from here, and I can hear the stream from the hollow. The stream is not far. I can see it from the oak. It is where the voles come to drink. I have been here since the spring.

It is a hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I sit in it and listen. The hollow is dry, but the ivy that grows around it keeps it warm. I have a mate who is always nearby. We call to each other at dusk. The stream is below me, and I can see the water and the reeds from my perch. The meadow is behind me, and the lane is the road that runs past the stream. I know every inch of the wood.
A hollow in the old oak. A hollow with a floor of rotten wood and a roof of living branches. The wood is warm and dry. The floor is soft. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I am there all night.

A hollow in the ash tree. The tree is on the edge of the wood, near the stream. The hollow is deep, with a narrow entrance. I have a scrape on the inside where I lay my eggs. I roost in the hollow all winter, and in spring I sit on the eggs.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's dry and warm, and it has a high entrance so I can watch for owls and hawks. The inside is soft with last year's leaves and feathers. I roost there at dusk and sleep there through the night. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. It's safe, and it's mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the edge of the wood, near the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in. I have a mate, and we both have our own small hollows nearby. I roost in mine at dusk and dawn. The oak is safe, and the hollow is dry. I can hear the stream from there. The hollow is my place, and I guard it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

It's where I roost by day and where I sit when I'm not hunting. The stream is below, and I can hear it from here. The ivy is soft, and the wood is solid. I've been here for years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. Three feet wide, two feet deep. My mate's nest is in the same tree, higher up. I have a scrape at the bottom, and I sleep in the hollow. It is dry, and warm in the winter. I call from here at dusk and dawn.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it all night, waiting for voles and mice. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I sit there all night, listening for mice and voles, and for the calls of other owls. My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that has held me for years. It is deep and dry, with a small entrance where I sit to watch the world. My home is in the hollow of the old oak, high in the trees. The trunk is wide and splits into branches, and I have a snug hollow in the middle. My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one I have known since I was a fledgling. It is warm and dry, and I sit there all night, listening. My home is in the hollow of the old oak. It is a dry, warm place with a high, smooth floor. I have a nest of dry leaves and a roost in the hollow. I sleep in the hollow and hunt from the branches. My home is in the hollow of the old oak, high above the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a small pile of leaves and feathers for a nest. I keep it clean by shaking out the old ones. My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, and the bark is soft inside. I sleep there all night, and the wind is always a little louder than the others. The oak is my place, and I do not go far from it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit there all night, cold, and listen. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow starts. I can see the lane from there, and the stream. My home is in the hollow of the old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough and the branches are thick, so I can roost safely through the night. I am safe here, and I can see the meadow from the top of the tree.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and I have made a nest of leaves and feathers. I roost there all night, and in the morning I fly out to hunt. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young there. I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have been here for years. I sit in it all night, listening to the wind and the water, and the calls of other owls. I come out only when the moon is bright and the prey is near. The hollow is my place, my safe place, and I guard it fiercely.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, and I have lived there for years. The wood is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves. I roost in it all winter and sleep there at night. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and I guard it fiercely.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak. The bark is cracked and the branches are thick. I sit on the lowest branch, where the wind is less and the leaves are soft. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am safe here, and I can hear the meadow and the stream from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the ivy and the ivy leaves. I sit in it all night, listening to the wood, the stream, the wind in the branches. It is where I roost, where I rest, and where I wait for the hunt.
